title: Loosely comparing uncomparable objects to booleans no longer depends on literal-vs-variable syntax
summary: As of PHP 8.5, loosely comparing an "uncomparable" object - an enum case, a `\CurlHandle`, or another internal class without its own comparison handler - to a boolean with `==`/`!=` is consolidated to always match `(bool) $object`. Before 8.5, and still today on PHP 8.4.19 (verified directly), the identical object gives opposite answers depending only on the syntactic shape of the boolean operand: `$object == true` (a bare literal) agrees with `(bool) $object`, while `$object == $variable` - holding the same value `true` - always returns `false` instead.
new_code_policy: Never compare an enum case, a `\CurlHandle`, or any other object to `true`/`false` with `==` or `!=`, and never let one reach a `switch`/`case` on the expectation that it detects truthiness. On a PHP 8.5+ floor the literal-vs-variable inconsistency this rule documents is gone - `==` and `!=` against a boolean now always agree with `(bool) $object` no matter how the boolean operand is written - but this catalog also has to serve floors below 8.5, where the same source line keeps its pre-8.5, syntax-dependent answer. Write `(bool) $object === $flag` (cast explicitly, then compare with `===`) wherever the intent is "does this object's truthiness equal this known boolean"; write a bare `if ($object)` / `if (!$object)` wherever the intent is simply "is this object truthy". Both forms give the identical, version-stable answer on every PHP minor this catalog tracks, including 8.5, and neither depends on whether the comparison target is a literal, a variable, a property, an array element, or a class constant.
existing_code_policy:
Search for `==`/`!=` comparisons, and `switch`/`match` discriminants, where one side can hold an enum case, a `\CurlHandle`/`\CurlMultiHandle`, a `\GdImage`, an `\XMLParser`, or another internal "resource-turned-object" class, and the other side is `true`, `false`, or an expression that evaluates to one. Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19 with `set_error_handler()` installed (no diagnostic of any kind was raised by any comparison below): for `$enum = Suit::Hearts;` (a plain, non-backed enum case), `(bool) $enum` is `true`; `$enum == true` (bare literal) is `true`, agreeing with the cast; `$enum == $trueVar` (the identical value, held in a variable) is `false`, disagreeing with the cast - the same value, the opposite answer, purely because of how the right-hand side is written. Reversing operand order changes nothing (`true == $enum` and `$trueVar == $enum` match the un-reversed forms). `!=` inherits the same split, being the plain negation of `==`: `$enum != true` is `false`, `$enum != $trueVar` is `true`. The spaceship operator, `<=>`, is unaffected by any of this: both `$enum <=> true` and `$enum <=> $trueVar` evaluate to `1` regardless of form.

The identical literal/variable split, with the same values, was independently reproduced for a real `\CurlHandle` (`curl_init()`), a `\GdImage` (`imagecreate()`), and an `\XMLParser` (`xml_parser_create()`) - confirming this is not enum-specific, but is specific to the "uncomparable" category UPGRADING names. `stdClass`, an anonymous userland class, `\DateTime`, `\SplStack`, a `Closure`, a `\Fiber`, and a `\ReflectionClass` instance were all separately verified to disagree with none of this: `== true` and `== $trueVar` (and `== false` / `== $falseVar`) agree with `(bool) $object` identically in both forms for every one of those, so ordinary objects and internal classes that implement a real comparison handler are not part of this bug and need no changes here.

The safe (cast-agreeing) side of this split is wider than "a bare token", and the boundary is not the one a reader would guess. Verified directly, each form measured as its own standalone statement (nesting the same expression inside an array literal can itself change the answer - see below, and the notes): a bare `true`/`false` token agrees with the cast, and so do a parenthesized literal `(true)`/`((true))`, a negation of a literal `!false`, a literal strict comparison `(1 === 1)`, a literal boolean conjunction `true && true`, and - independently and unexpectedly - a scalar class constant, whether referenced as `self::EXPECTED` from inside its declaring class or as `Flags::DEFAULT_ENABLED` from outside it (confirmed directly, reproducibly across repeated runs). But a *global* constant - `const GLOBAL_CONST_TRUE = true;` or `define('DEFINED_CONST_TRUE', true)` - reproduces the *disagreeing* answer, indistinguishable from a plain variable, as does a ternary that trivially resolves to `true` (`true ? true : false`), a `(bool)` cast of a literal (`(bool) 1`), a property read, an array element, and a function-call return value. Do not assume a symbol named as a constant is safe: confirm whether it is a class constant (safe here) or a global one (not safe here) before deciding a call site is fine as-is. This catalog records what was measured for each of these forms, not why the engine draws the line where it does.

`switch`/`case` does not reliably reproduce the cast-agreeing answer either, in a way that is easy to get backwards. `switch ($enum) { case true: }` and `switch ($enum) { case $trueVar: }` - the natural way to write "branch on this object's truthiness" - both fail to match on this host, agreeing with the *disagreeing* `==` form regardless of whether the case arm is a literal or a variable. `switch (true) { case $enum: }` does match, but that reflects the well-known `switch(true)`-as-if-chain idiom (each case arm read as its own boolean condition, not compared against the switch subject via this mechanism), not a confirmed instance of the same literal-vs-variable behavior, and this catalog does not recommend relying on it as a workaround. `match(true) { $enum => ... }` never matches, in any form, because `match` compares with strict `===` throughout and no object is ever `===` to a boolean - internally consistent, but not a working substitute for testing truthiness. Treat `==`, `!=`, `switch`/`case`, and `match` alike as unsafe for testing these objects against a boolean, and replace each affected call site with an explicit `(bool)` cast compared using `===`.
guideline: Never rely on `==`/`!=` (or a `switch`/`case` discriminant) to test an enum case, a `\CurlHandle`, or another "uncomparable" internal object against a boolean; verified directly, the exact same object gives opposite answers today depending only on how the boolean side is written - a bare literal, a parenthesized or logically-trivial literal expression, and a class constant all agree with `(bool) $object`, while a variable, a global constant, a property, an array element, a ternary, and a function-call return value all disagree. Cast explicitly and compare with `===` instead: `(bool) $object === $flag` gives the identical, version-stable answer regardless of how `$flag` is written, on every PHP minor this catalog tracks.
details:
UPGRADING-8.5.0 lists this under Backward Incompatible Changes -> Core: "Loosely comparing uncomparable objects (e.g. enums, \CurlHandle and other internal classes) to booleans was previously inconsistent. If compared to a boolean literal $object == true, it would behave the same way as (bool) $object. If compared to a statically unknown value $object == $true, it would always return false. This behavior was consolidated to always follow the behavior of (bool) $object."

Verified directly on PHP 8.4.19 with `set_error_handler()` installed (no diagnostic was ever raised by any comparison described here): for a plain enum case `$enum = Suit::Hearts;`, `(bool) $enum` is `true`. `$enum == true` (a bare literal) agrees with the cast (`true`); `$enum == $trueVar`, where `$trueVar` holds the identical value `true`, disagrees with the cast (`false`) - the same value, the opposite answer, purely because of how the right-hand side is written. Reversing operand order changes nothing (`true == $enum` and `$trueVar == $enum` match the un-reversed forms). `!=` inherits the same split, being the plain negation of `==`. The spaceship operator, `<=>`, is unaffected by any of this: both `$enum <=> true` and `$enum <=> $trueVar` evaluate to `1` regardless of form. The identical literal/variable split was independently reproduced for a real `\CurlHandle` (`curl_init()`), a `\GdImage` (`imagecreate()`), and an `\XMLParser` (`xml_parser_create()`) - confirming this is not enum-specific, but is specific to the "uncomparable" category UPGRADING names: `stdClass`, an anonymous class, `\DateTime`, `\SplStack`, a `Closure`, a `\Fiber`, and a `\ReflectionClass` instance were all separately verified to agree with `(bool) $object` in both the literal and the variable form, with no inconsistency at all - ordinary objects, and internal classes that implement a real comparison handler, are simply not affected.

The agreeing side of the split is wider than "a bare literal" alone: verified directly, each form measured as its own standalone statement, a parenthesized literal (`(true)`, `((true))`), a negation of a literal (`!false`), a literal strict comparison (`(1 === 1)`), a literal boolean conjunction (`true && true`), and - independently and unexpectedly - a scalar class constant (`self::EXPECTED` from inside its declaring class, or `Flags::DEFAULT_ENABLED` from outside it) all agree with the cast exactly like a bare `true`/`false` token. A *global* constant declared with `const GLOBAL_CONST_TRUE = true;` or `define('DEFINED_CONST_TRUE', true)`, a ternary that trivially resolves to `true` (`true ? true : false`), a `(bool)` cast of a literal (`(bool) 1`), a property read, an array element, and a function-call return value were all separately verified to disagree with the cast exactly like a plain variable. A reviewer who assumes "it's a named constant, so it's fine" can be looking at either side of this split; this catalog records what was measured for each form without asserting why the engine draws the line here rather than somewhere else. `switch`/`case` compounds the hazard rather than offering an escape: `switch ($enum) { case true: }` and `switch ($enum) { case $trueVar: }` - the natural way to write this check - both fail to match on this host, agreeing with the *disagreeing* `==` form regardless of whether the case arm is a literal or a variable; only the unrelated `switch (true) { case $enum: }` idiom (case arms read as their own boolean conditions, not compared against the switch subject) happened to match here, and this catalog does not rely on that as a confirmed instance of the same mechanism or recommend it as a workaround. `match(true) { $enum => ... }` never matches in any form, because `match` compares with strict `===` throughout and no object is ever `===` to a boolean; internally consistent, but not a working substitute for testing truthiness.

The version-stable fix is to stop asking `==`/`!=` (or `switch`/`match`) to do this at all: cast explicitly and, if a specific known boolean must be matched, compare the cast result with `===` - `(bool) $object === $flag` was verified directly to return the identical, correct answer regardless of whether `$flag` is a literal or a variable. Here `introduced_in` is set to 8.5 because that is the minor this behavior actually changed in - the field exists so this behavior_change rule can be range-gated on the feature axis, and it is not a claim that PHP 8.5 introduced enums, `\CurlHandle`, or the `==` operator itself, all of which existed well before 8.5.
notes: Runtime matrix executed on PHP 8.4.19 (2026-09-06) with `set_error_handler()` installed (no `[errno=...]` line was ever printed, confirming zero diagnostics throughout): $enum = Suit::Hearts (plain enum case) => (bool) $enum = true; $enum == true = true; $enum == $trueVar = false; $enum == false = false; $enum == $falseVar = false; $enum != true = false; $enum != $trueVar = true; $enum <=> true = 1; $enum <=> $trueVar = 1 (spaceship unaffected). Operand order confirmed irrelevant: true == $enum = true, $trueVar == $enum = false - identical to the un-reversed forms. A backed enum case (StringSuit::Hearts) reproduced the identical split. A real \CurlHandle from curl_init() reproduced the identical split and values.

Right-hand-side shape sweep, re-measured directly on PHP 8.4.19 (2026-09-06), each form as its own standalone statement ($rN = $enum == <form>;), and reproduced identically across two full runs: true, (true), ((true)), !false, (1 === 1), true && true, and a class constant referenced either externally (Flags::DEFAULT_ENABLED, a separate final class) or internally (self::EXPECTED, read inside a method of the class that declares it) all AGREE with (bool) $enum. A global const (const G_TRUE = true;), define('D_TRUE', true), a plain variable, a typed property ($o->t), an array element ($a['t']), a function-call return value (rt()), a ternary (true ? true : false), and a (bool) cast of a literal ((bool) 1) all DISAGREE. An earlier draft of this rule classified the parenthesized-literal form as disagreeing; that measurement had actually compared $enum against a variable that was first assigned from (true) (a separate statement), not against (true) written directly in the comparison - a different thing to measure, corrected here.

Observation on measurement methodology, reproduced deterministically across two runs: the same written expression can evaluate to a different answer depending on where it sits, independent of the enum or boolean value involved. $direct = $enum == (true ? true : false); as its own statement gives the disagreeing answer (false), but the byte-identical expression evaluated as an array literal's value, ['k' => $enum == (true ? true : false)], gives the agreeing answer (true) for that element - confirmed on a fresh enum instance and on repeat runs. This was not found to reproduce for every form tried inside an array literal: a plain variable and a global constant gave the same, disagreeing answer whether tested as a standalone statement or inside an array literal. This catalog does not attempt to explain why; it is recorded because it means a probe written to check this rule's own claims can return a false all-clear (or a false alarm) purely from how the probe itself is written, so every row in the sweep above was measured as its own standalone statement rather than collected into a table or array.

switch/match, verified directly: switch ($enum) { case true: } => no match; switch ($enum) { case $trueVar: } => no match (both agree with the disagreeing `==` path). switch (true) { case $enum: } => matched; switch ($trueVar) { case $enum: } => no match. match (true) { $enum => 'x', default => 'y' } => always the default arm (match's strict === comparison never treats an object as identical to a boolean, in any form tested).

Unaffected-object control, verified directly: stdClass, an anonymous class with a public property, \DateTime, \SplStack, a Closure, a \Fiber, and a \ReflectionClass instance all agree with (bool) $object for both `== true` (literal) and `== $trueVar` (variable), with no inconsistency - confirming the bug is specific to the "uncomparable" category UPGRADING names (enums and certain internal resource-wrapper-turned-objects), not to objects in general. \GdImage (from imagecreate(1, 1)) and \XMLParser (from xml_parser_create()) were separately confirmed to belong to the affected "uncomparable" category alongside enums and \CurlHandle, reproducing the identical literal-vs-variable split.

PHPCompatibility 10.0.0-alpha2 was run directly (2026-09-06) via `<analyzer>/vendor/bin/phpcs --standard=PHPCompatibility --runtime-set testVersion 8.2-8.5 --report=json --parallel=1 --extensions=php --severity=1 --no-cache -q <probe-dir>` against files containing an enum compared to a bool with == inside a class method, and a \CurlHandle compared to a bool variable and a literal, and produced zero findings ({"errors": 0, "warnings": 0}); verification.phpcompatibility is therefore intentionally empty rather than guessed. This is the structural blindness described in the round's shared contract: PHPCompatibility's sniffs check version-availability facts about functions, constants, and syntax, not a runtime value-comparison outcome that depends on operand syntax, so a clean phpcs run gives no signal about any of the above.

Evidence: UPGRADING-8.5.0, "1. Backward Incompatible Changes" -> Core: "Loosely comparing uncomparable objects (e.g. enums, \CurlHandle and other internal classes) to booleans was previously inconsistent. If compared to a boolean literal $object == true, it would behave the same way as (bool) $object. If compared to a statically unknown value $object == $true, it would always return false. This behavior was consolidated to always follow the behavior of (bool) $object."
